Opcode Column
Represents the literal byte value(s) which correspond to the given instruction
In this case, if you were to see a 0x24 followed by a byte, or 0x25 followed by 4 bytes, you would know they were specific forms of the AND instruction
For more detail, see Intel Vol. 2a section 3.1.1.1
“Opcode Column in the Instruction Summary Table (Instructions without VEX Prefix)”
If it was 0x25, how would you know whether it should be followed by 2 bytes (imm16) or 4 bytes (imm32)?
The length of the operand depends on if the processor is in 16-bit, 32-bit, or 64-bit mode
Each mode has a default operand size (i.e. the size of the value)
There are many instructions which are “overloaded” with equivalent 16 bit and 32 bit versions shown in the manual.
For 64-bit mode, the default operand size is 32-bits for most instructions and the default address size is 64-bits
This means the default interpretation will usually be the ones with the r/m32, r32, imm32, or in this case a specific register like EAX, unless explicitly overridden with special instruction prefixes
These are talked about later in optional material
There are many instructions which are “overloaded” with equivalent 16 bit and 32 bit versions shown in the manual.
Instruction Column
The human-readable mnemonic which is used to represent the instruction.
This will frequently contain special encodings such as the “r/mX format” which I’ve previously discussed
For more detail, see Intel Vol. 2a section 3.1.1.3
“Instruction Column in the Opcode Summary Table”
"Operand Encoding" Column
Indicates what forms the operands can take
For more detail, see Intel Vol. 2a section 3.1.1.4
“Operand Encoding Column in the Instruction Summary Table”
Whether or not the opcode is valid in 64 bit mode
For more detail, see Intel Vol. 2a section 3.1.1.5
“64/32-bit Mode Column in the Instruction Summary Table”
Should say "Valid" and "Invalid"
Compatibility/Legacy Mode Column
Whether or not the opcode is valid in 32/16 bit code
For more detail, see Intel Vol. 2a section 3.1.1.5
“64/32-bit Mode Column in the Instruction Summary Table”
Should say "Valid" and "Invalid"
Description Column
Simple description of the action performed by the instruction
Typically this just conveys the flavor of the instruction, but the majority of the details are in the main description text
See Intel Vol. 2a section 3.1.1.7
“Description Column in the Instruction Summary Table”

AND Details
Less Obvious
It turns out that for instructions that set status flags (e.g. arithmetic operations), the hardware just does the operation and sets flags as if the operands were both unsigned and signed
Basically the hardware doesn’t know or care about whether the humans are currently interpreting the bits as signed or unsigned. That’s the compiler’s problem to sort out.
The compiler must emit instructions which treat the bits as signed or unsigned based on what’s specified in the high level language
Jcc Revisited
If you look closely, you will see that there are multiple mnemonics for the same opcodes. The opcodes prove they're the same instructions
Which mnemonic is displayed is disassembler-dependent
Jcc Revisited
A "short" control flow displacement is always specified by a signed 8-bit number
A "near" control flow displacement could be a signed 16-bit (except when running in 64-bit mode) or signed 32-bit number

There's no "call short"
"Absolute indirect" form calculates an absolute address, using either just an address in a register, or an address calculated with the r/m64 "base + index*scale + displacement" form
"Far" control flow transfer involves the specification of a "segment selector". We learn about those in Arch2001

RET supports both "near" & "far" control flow transfer. But you'll almost only ever see the near return (0xC3)
